title: Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification

summaries.example: Imagine two students who see what looks like a dog. They have exactly the same thoughts and experiences. One is looking at a real dog; the other is looking at a very clever robot. An internalist may say their reasons for believing “There is a dog” are the same because their experiences are the same. An externalist may say the real connection to the world can also matter.
summaries.summary: This entry explains a disagreement in epistemology, the study of knowledge. Internalists say that what makes a belief justified must depend on the thinker’s own mental life or on reasons the thinker can access by reflection. Externalists deny that this must always be so. They argue that outside facts—such as whether a belief-forming method reliably connects belief with truth—may matter. The debate includes unusual abilities, duties and responsibility, evidence, memory, testimony, and the “new evil demon” case, in which someone is deceived but has the same experiences as a person who sees the world accurately. The entry also warns that philosophers may be using different ideas of “justification,” so some disagreements may concern what role justification is supposed to play.
key_ideas: Internalists focus on a thinker’s thoughts, experiences, and available reasons.
Externalists say that connections to the world may also matter, such as whether a way of forming beliefs usually gets things right.
A person might have a true belief by luck, so truth alone may not be enough for knowledge.
Philosophers disagree about whether justification is the same as being rational, responsible, or following an epistemic duty.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often need to decide whether a belief is well supported, not merely whether it happens to be true. This debate helps us think carefully about evidence, memory, trustworthy methods, and the difference between a lucky guess and knowledge. It also shows why people can disagree even when they share the same basic examples: they may be asking different questions about reasons, truth, responsibility, or the thinker’s connection with reality.

important_terms.definition: A belief is justified when a person has good enough grounds for holding it.
The view that justification depends only on what is inside a thinker’s mind or available from that thinker’s point of view.
The view that something outside the thinker’s point of view can help determine whether a belief is justified.
Information, experiences, or reasons that support a belief.
A belief-producing way of thinking that usually leads to true beliefs, such as careful seeing in normal conditions.

questions_to_think_about: If two people have exactly the same experiences, should they always have the same justification?
Is a true guess justified if the person had no good reason for it?
Can a person responsibly keep a belief after forgetting why they first believed it?
Should a reliable skill count as a good reason even when the person cannot explain how it works?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya remembers that a science book said broccoli can support heart health, but she no longer remembers the source or the evidence. An externalist might explain her present justification partly through the reliability of her memory and the quality of the original learning. An internalist may instead look for something present in her experience—such as a memory impression—or argue that it is not irresponsible for her to rely on memory when she has no reason to doubt it. A related problem arises if another person formed the same belief from a bad source and later forgot that source: should the two people now be equally justified if they are internally alike?
summaries.summary: The entry examines internalist and externalist theories of epistemic justification. Internalism is usually presented as a supervenience claim: if two thinkers are alike in the relevant internal respects, then the same propositions are justified for them. The internal may be understood accessibly—as what reflection can reveal—or mentally—as what depends on the thinker’s mental life. Externalism rejects the requirement that justification be fixed in this way, while allowing that some theories combine internal and external conditions. Arguments for internalism use cases of clairvoyance, the normative and guiding role of justification, evidentialism, and the new evil demon scenario. Arguments for externalism stress justification’s connection with truth, the need to explain stored beliefs and childhood testimony, and epistemic norms whose application may depend on external facts. The entry does not present a final resolution; it emphasizes that the debate is complicated by different ideas of justification, rationality, responsibility, warrant, and knowledge.
key_ideas: The target of the entry is mainly justification, not the separate question of whether knowledge itself requires an internal condition.
Internalists typically defend a supervenience thesis: internally identical thinkers have the same propositional justification.
“Internal” can mean mentally constituted or reflectively accessible, and these definitions may not coincide.
Internalist arguments appeal to guidance, rationality, responsibility, duty, evidence, and the intuition that a deceived thinker can be just as justified as we are.
Externalist arguments appeal to truth-connections, explanatory power, reliable memory and testimony, and norms that may refer to facts outside the thinker’s perspective.
The disagreement may partly reflect different conceptions of justification, including subjective and objective standards.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we evaluate perception, memory, testimony, scientific reasoning, and beliefs formed under deception. It asks whether good reasoning is determined by the believer’s perspective or also by the way belief connects with reality. The debate also separates several questions that are easily confused: whether a belief is justified, whether it is rational or responsible, whether it is reliably formed, and whether it qualifies as knowledge. Keeping these questions apart can make disagreements about evidence and belief more precise.

important_terms.definition: A theory about whether justification is fixed by internal conditions, such that internal duplicates have the same justification.
A theory denying that justification is fixed entirely by internal conditions; external factors may contribute.
The claim that changes in justification require changes in the relevant internal conditions; internal duplicates therefore match in justification.
The view that justification depends on what is reflectively available to the thinker.
The view that justification depends on relevant aspects of a thinker’s mental life, whether or not all are accessible.
The view that a thinker’s evidence determines what the thinker is justified in believing.
A property of a belief-forming process that tends to produce true beliefs under relevant conditions.
A thought experiment in which a deceiver makes someone’s experiences misleading while preserving the person’s internal perspective.

questions_to_think_about: Does a reliable belief-forming method justify a belief if the thinker cannot identify the method or its reliability?
Should a person who formed a belief badly but later forgets the original reason receive an epistemic “upgrade”?
Do the new evil demon cases show that justification is internal, or only that justification differs from warrant or knowledge?
Can a norm for belief require something that the believer cannot determine by reflection?
Are internalism and externalism competing over one notion of justification or several?

summaries.example: Jordan learns from a teacher that a certain local plant is safe to touch. Years later, Jordan remembers the claim but forgets the lesson and has no notes. An externalist might say the reliability of Jordan’s memory and the original source help explain why the belief remains justified. An internalist might say Jordan’s present memory experience or lack of any warning is enough. Now imagine another student who formed the same belief from a prank website and later forgot that fact. If both students now seem mentally identical, should their beliefs have the same status? Philosophers use cases like this to test their theories.
summaries.summary: This entry studies whether epistemic justification depends entirely on a thinker’s internal perspective. Internalists defend a supervenience principle: relevantly identical thinkers should have identical justification. They may define the internal through mental states or through what a thinker can access by reflection. Externalists reject this restriction. They may hold that reliability, the thinker’s history, the environment, or other truth-related facts help determine justification, sometimes alongside internal conditions. The entry surveys influential arguments on both sides. Clairvoyance cases question whether an unexplained ability can provide justification. Arguments from duty, rationality, responsibility, and evidence support internalist ideas about guidance and control. The new evil demon objection holds that a deceived person may be just as justified as an ordinary person despite lacking a successful connection to truth. Externalists respond with arguments about truth-conduciveness, explanatory adequacy, memory, childhood testimony, and norms governing belief. The entry concludes that progress may require deciding which role or notion of justification is at issue.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes the debate about justification from the broader debate about whether knowledge needs an internal condition.
Internalists usually say that internal duplicates—thinkers alike in relevant internal respects—must have the same justification.
Externalists can accept that both internal and external conditions are needed; externalism does not have to be purely external.
The clairvoyance case challenges the idea that a reliable but unexplained ability automatically gives justification.
The evil demon case suggests that someone whose experiences are systematically misleading may still be as justified as someone whose experiences are accurate.
Externalists argue that reliability, memory history, testimony, and truth-related norms may explain facts that internalism struggles to explain.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate helps explain why a true belief can be a lucky guess, why reliable methods seem important, and why deception seems not to remove all rational support. It is relevant whenever we assess claims based on perception, memory, testimony, or expert skill. It also teaches a broader lesson about philosophical arguments: a thought experiment may test several concepts at once, and a disagreement may continue because the participants assign different jobs to the word “justified.”

important_terms.definition: The idea that a belief is supported by reasons or conditions that make it reasonable for a thinker to hold.
The position that justification is determined by internal features of the thinker, such as mental states or accessible reasons.
The position that justification can depend partly on external features, such as reliability or the belief’s relation to truth.
A relation in which one set of facts fixes another: if the first facts are the same, the second facts cannot differ.
The view that evidence determines what a person is justified in believing.
The tendency of a method or process to produce true beliefs rather than false ones.
A type of justification concerning whether there is support for a proposition, whether or not the person actually believes it.
A type of justification involving an actual belief held on the right basis.

questions_to_think_about: If a person has the same experiences as you but lives in a deceptive world, are their beliefs equally justified?
Is a belief justified because it is rational from the person’s point of view, because it is reliably formed, or both?
Can someone have knowledge without justification, or justification without knowledge?
What should count as evidence when a person sees something accurately versus merely seeming to see it?
Does forgetting an original reason change the justification of a continuing belief?
